Article Title: An Oklahoma man allegedly claimed he inherited a $5.4 million mansion, tried three times to record a deed and had electricity moved into his name; county clerks refused the filings and he now faces tw
Article Text:
Representative image

What investigators say happened

Three refused deed filings

The felony charges

Why deed fraud is a problem

How owners can protect themselves

An Oklahoma man allegedly tried to claim ownership of a $5.4 million mansion by insisting he had inherited it from deceased relatives, but county clerks refused to record the paperwork he repeatedly submitted. According to the Oklahoma County Sheriff’s Office, 29-year-old Antonio Moore attempted three times to file a deed for the roughly 14,000-square-foot property in Oklahoma City’s gated Gaillardia neighborhood. The situation escalated after the legitimate homeowner discovered that electricity service had been moved into Moore’s name and that a bank had flagged an attempted loan using the mansion as collateral. Moore was arrested on September 30 and now faces two felony charges, including first-degree forgery and obtaining property by deception. The allegations remain unproven in court, and he is presumed innocent unless convicted. The case, first reported by Wealth of Geeks and local Oklahoma outlets, highlights how property-title fraud can begin with paperwork that looks official but fails basic verification. Read more details about it here:The first reported incident occurred in April, when the homeowner’s association contacted the property owner after a man tried to enter the gated community and claimed the mansion had belonged to relatives who had died. Community security did not allow him inside, according to a sheriff’s report cited by KFOR. The man reportedly attempted to enter Gaillardia twice more during that same month. Sheriff Tommie Johnson III later publicly described the investigation on October 22, identifying the residence as a large home in the exclusive neighborhood. These early encounters became important because they reportedly preceded the more formal attempt to establish ownership through county records.The homeowner then began receiving correspondence addressed to Moore at the mansion, which raised further concerns. He also learned that electricity service had been transferred into Moore’s name, an unusual development for a property he still owned. According to the sheriff’s office, Bank of Oklahoma notified the homeowner about an attempted loan that used the residence as collateral. Johnson told KOCO that he believed Moore’s intended objective was to borrow money against the property. In other words, investigators allege that the claimed inheritance may have been part of an effort to make the mansion appear available for financing.On September 11, employees at the Oklahoma County Clerk’s Office alerted sheriff’s deputies after receiving paperwork that purported to show Moore had inherited the mansion, as per reports. The legitimate homeowner also went to the office to report possible fraud. Clerk’s office staff reviewed the documents carefully, explained why they could not be recorded, and asked additional questions, according to information reported by FOX 25. Despite that refusal, investigators said Moore returned to the office twice more with similar paperwork. The repeated filings ultimately became central evidence in the case described by the sheriff’s office.A deed does not automatically create lawful ownership simply because someone prepares or presents it. County recording offices generally assess whether documents meet filing requirements, but they do not adjudicate every underlying ownership dispute. In this instance, employees declined to record the disputed deed, preventing it from entering the official land records. Sheriff Johnson warned that even if an unauthorized document is recorded, it can complicate later title searches and property transactions. Clearing such a record may require legal proceedings, which is why early detection matters for homeowners.Oklahoma County court records identify the defendant as Antonio D Shay Moore and show that prosecutors filed two felony counts on September 30. The first count is first-degree forgery under Oklahoma law, while the second alleges obtaining property by trick, deception, or false representation. The court docket for State of Oklahoma v. Antonio D Shay Moore, case CF-2026-5325, records an initial appearance on October 6. A judge set bail at $25,000 and tentatively appointed a public defender. A preliminary-hearing conference was scheduled for October 27 at 9 a.m, reported Wealth of Geeks.It is important to distinguish an allegation from a conviction. Moore has not been found guilty, and the charges will need to be proven through the normal legal process. The sheriff’s office has described its investigation and the alleged pattern of conduct, but the court will determine what evidence is admissible and whether the prosecution meets its burden. Until then, the case should be understood as an accusation involving alleged document fraud and an attempted property-related deception.Property-title fraud often involves making it look like a valid transfer occurred, rather than actually taking possession of a house. Forged signatures, false inheritance claims, unauthorized liens and fraudulent deeds can all create confusion for banks, buyers, title companies and county officials. While such a document, if filed, may not immediately transfer ownership, it can cloud the title and make a future sale or refinance more difficult. This is of particular concern for high value properties where a successful fraud attempt could potentially underpin a large loan application.The Oklahoma Real Estate Commission’s 2026 deed-theft notice identifies several warning signs, including unsolicited mortgage or utility mail, unauthorized deeds, and unexpected loans connected to a property. It advises owners to examine county land records and investigate suspicious notices promptly. Homeowners should also monitor their credit reports for unfamiliar loans and contact the county clerk or an attorney if a deed or lien appears without authorization. Anyone who believes they have been targeted should report the matter to law enforcement.Oklahoma County offers a Property Alert System that sends registered users notifications when documents affecting their property are filed. Alerts can arrive by text message, email, or telephone, giving owners an early warning before a suspicious filing goes unnoticed. The system cannot stop someone from submitting paperwork, but it can help a homeowner respond quickly. In this case, the combination of alert clerk employees, a vigilant homeowner, and law-enforcement involvement appears to have prevented the disputed deed from being recorded.The alleged Oklahoma mansion case is a reminder that ownership is not established by confidence, repeated claims, or a document presented at a counter. It is subject to legal title, to verifiable records and due process. For homeowners, the practical takeaway is that any surprise utility changes, loan inquiries or mail for someone who doesn’t live at their address should be considered a potential red flag. For counties and lenders, the case underscores the value of careful document review before property records or financing decisions are affected.
Article Summary: Oklahoma man allegedly tried to claim ownership of a $5.4 million mansion by insisting he had inherited it from deceased relatives. County clerks refused to record the paperwork he repeatedly submitted. The situation escalated after the homeowner discovered that electricity service had been moved into Moore’s name and that a bank had flagged an attempted loan.

Article Title: In 2022, Arsenal star Bukayo Saka funded 120 operations for children in Nigeria; four years later, his work with a charity that restored a Rwandan boy's sight has earned him the 2026 Socrates Award in
Article Text:
Saka continues supporting underprivileged children through Big Shoe, providing access to healthcare, opportunities and brighter futures.

A recognition outside of football

Nigeria: 120 children

Restoring a child’s vision

A wide-ranging mission

A different type of win

Football’s biggest moments are often measured by goals, trophies and memorable nites under stadium lights. But for Bukayo Saka, one of the most meaningful victories has come away from the pitch, in hospitals, classrooms and communities where access to basic medical care can transform a child’s future. The Arsenal star’s continued humanitarian efforts have now earned him one of football’s biggest off-pitch honors. Scroll down to find out the details of his humanitarian act.Saka was named the winner of the 2026 Socrates Award at the Ballon d’Or ceremony in London, an award given to footballers whose humanitarian contributions extend beyond the sport, according to a report by The Cable. The prize, named in honor of the legendary Brazilian footballer, was first given in 2022 to former Liverpool forward Sadio Mane and has since become a major recognition of the role football plays in supporting social causes.The Standard reports Saka was recognized for his extensive humanitarian work with his family and several charitable organizations, particularly his long-standing involvement with Big Shoe, which provides medical assistance and humanitarian support to children and families in need around the world. The award was presented by Nigerian musician Burna Boy at the gala, held at the Palladium Theater in London, adds The Cable.Saka has worked with Big Shoe on initiatives to support children who may have trouble accessing necessary medical procedures, according to The Standard. In 2022, the Arsenal winger partnered with the charity to finance life-changing surgeries for 120 children in Kano, Nigeria, in one of the most significant efforts of his charitable work to date.His support went beyond Nigeria the following year. Saka also helped fund surgeries for another 100 children across Rwanda, Kenya and Tanzania, as part of broader efforts to bring critical healthcare to children in developing communities, The Cable reported. The work has a personal resonance with the cause. Saka, who is of Nigerian heritage, has long used his platform to support initiatives for children in worlds of situations from his own.Among the stories featured around Saka’s Socrates Award was that of 14-year-old Biringiro from Rwanda, whose eyesight was restored thanks to Big Shoe’s medical program. Biringiro had started losing his sight at the age of 12, The Standard reports. Living in a village without electricity, his failing eyesight had made it increasingly difficult to move around each day and had impacted his ability to fully participate at school.Thanks to treatment supported by Big Shoe, the young boy was able to regain his sight and go back to activities that had become difficult, including reading the classroom blackboard. His story was a powerful testament to the impact behind Saka’s charitable work, turning the award from a personal achievement into recognition of the children and communities benefitting from the initiative.Saka’s humanitarian efforts go beyond individual medical procedures. The footballer has been working with Big Shoe and his family to help children who do not have the same chances or resources as many others.The initiative also reflects the broader purpose of the Socrates Award: to highlight the ability of prominent athletes to use their visibility and influence to create meaningful change away from competition.Saka has emphasized the importance of helping children rediscover simple joys and possibilities that illness or poverty can take away, as The Standard reported. For young beneficiaries of Big Shoe’s work, that can mean something as fundamental as being able to see clearly, return to school or imagine a future without a medical condition that defines their possibilities.The 2026 Socrates Award adds another layer to Saka’s growing legacy. His footballing legacy with Arsenal may continue to define him, but his charitable work is creating an impact measured in lives, not in scorelines.Images Courtesy: Facebook and istock
Article Summary: Bukayo Saka was named the winner of the 2026 Socrates Award at the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London. The award is given to footballers whose humanitarian contributions extend beyond the sport. Saka has long supported Big Shoe, which provides medical assistance and humanitarian support to children and families in need around the world. In 2022, the Arsenal winger partnered with the charity to finance life-changing surgeries for 120 children in Nigeria.

Article Title: In 2018, musician Beck and his then-wife bought a 1939 Los Angeles house for $3.1 million; years later, the property once transformed on a TV renovation show, was sold to Robert Pattinson for $5.3 mil
Article Text:
A 1939 home with a Hollywood history

From television renovation to celebrity ownership

Inside the Spanish Colonial Revival house

Los Angeles' celebrity property market

A 1939 Spanish Colonial Revival house in Los Angeles, once owned by musician Beck and featured on a television renovation show, became the home of actor Robert Pattinson and his partner Suki Waterhouse after a reported $5.3 million purchase. The property, located in the Hollywood Hills, had been bought by Beck and his then-wife, actress Marissa Ribisi , for $3.1 million in 2018. Following the couple's divorce in 2021, Ribisi retained the home and later sold it to the actor and Waterhouse, according to Homes & Gardens. The transaction put the property back in the spotlight, not only because of its celebrity ownership history but also because of its architectural character and connection to the Bravo reality series 'Flipping Out'. The house was renovated by interior designer Jeff Lewis, whose work on the property was documented on the show.The house was built in 1939 and reflects the Spanish Colonial Revival style, an architectural tradition associated with stucco exteriors, arched details and an emphasis on indoor-outdoor living. According to Architectural Digest, the property measures approximately 2,725 square feet and includes three bedrooms and three-and-a-half bathrooms.Set on a sloping, landscaped lot, the house is concealed behind thick hedges and gates, providing privacy from the surrounding neighbourhood. Its position on the hillside gives the property a secluded feel despite its location in Los Angeles, where celebrity homes frequently attract attention from fans and real-estate watchers.The home was renovated by Lewis, who documented the process on 'Flipping Out'. The Bravo series followed the designer and his team as they transformed residential properties, often highlighting the decisions involved in balancing a home's existing features with updated interiors.The renovation added another layer to the house's story. It was not simply a residence changing hands between well-known owners; it was also a property that had already appeared on television before becoming part of Pattinson and Waterhouse's real-estate portfolio.Before Beck and Ribisi acquired the property, it belonged to Stephanie Savage, the television writer and producer known for co-creating 'Gossip Girl'. She purchased the house in 2014, according to Homes & Gardens. Beck, whose real name is Beck Hansen, and Ribisi bought the residence for $3.1 million in 2018. Ribisi is an actress known for appearances in films including 'Dazed and Confused'. The couple's ownership ended following their divorce in 2021, after which Ribisi held the property before its subsequent sale.Pattinson and Waterhouse purchased the house for $5.3 million, a price approximately $2.2 million higher than the amount Beck and Ribisi had paid five years earlier. The difference reflects the change in reported transaction prices, but it should not be treated as Beck's personal profit: Ribisi was the seller, and the calculation does not account for renovation expenses, taxes, transaction costs or other ownership costs.The purchase was reported by Architectural Digest in February 2023. The outlet identified Pattinson and Waterhouse as the buyers and detailed the property's previous owners, design history and features.The interiors combine traditional architectural elements with contemporary fittings. Dark hardwood floors run through the principal living areas, while vaulted ceilings with exposed wooden beams give the living room a sense of height. A large brick fireplace serves as a focal point, reinforcing the house's traditional character. The living room connects with the formal dining room, family room and kitchen, creating a layout suited to both everyday living and entertaining. The kitchen features dark cabinetry, marble countertops and high-end appliances, according to Homes & Gardens.The primary suite includes a walk-in closet and a private balcony overlooking the grounds. Other bedrooms and bathrooms provide additional accommodation within the relatively compact home, whose design makes use of the sloping site. Outside, the landscaped grounds include terraces, pathways and a patio area designed for outdoor dining. The property also features a plunge pool, spa and covered fireplace area. Dense greenery and boundary hedges provide privacy, while the outdoor spaces extend the home's living areas into the garden.The combination of historic details and modern amenities helped distinguish the property in coverage of Pattinson's purchase. Rather than a sprawling estate, it is a relatively modest-sized house whose appeal lies in its privacy, design and Hollywood history.The sale illustrates how Los Angeles homes can acquire a distinct identity through successive celebrity owners and appearances in entertainment programmes. The house's appeal rests on several overlapping histories: its pre-war architecture, Lewis's televised renovation, Savage's ownership and the later connection to Beck and Pattinson.For Pattinson, known for 'Twilight' and 'The Batman', the purchase added another Spanish-style residence to his Los Angeles property history. Waterhouse, a British model and singer, was also identified as a buyer in the 2023 reports.While the $5.3 million transaction drew attention because of the names associated with it, the property's appeal extends beyond celebrity ownership. Its Spanish Colonial Revival design, secluded hillside setting and mix of original architectural character and updated interiors made it a distinctive example of the residential architecture found in the Hollywood Hills.
Article Summary: Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse bought a 1939 Spanish Colonial Revival house in the Hollywood Hills for $5.3 million in February 2023. The property was once owned by musician Beck and his then-wife, actress Marissa Ribisi. The couple's ownership ended following their divorce in 2021, after which Ribisi held the property before its subsequent sale. The house was renovated by interior designer Jeff Lewis, whose work on the property was documented on the Bravo reality series 'Flipping Out'

Article Title: Disturbing video shows days-old baby monkeys tormented in experiments at the University of Washington; the six-year study, costing $4.2 million, involved 32 pregnant macaques and 28 separated infants;
Article Text:
Pic credit: Peta YouTube screengrab

Days-old baby monkeys separated from their mothers and killed after the experiment

Pic credit: Peta

Unethical experiments

Newly released footage from the animal rights group Peta shows infant macaques, some only two days old, separated from their mothers and subjected to neurological tests at the University of Washington’s National Primate Research Center (WaNPRC). The video offers the first filmed look inside these experiments. It shows tiny monkeys shrieking in fear and gripping blankets, their only form of comfort, as researchers shave their heads, attach electrodes and test their reflexes and memory to determine whether exposure to a neurotoxin in the womb has damaged their developing brains. Peta obtained the video through a records request in September 2026. It was filmed between 2017 and 2019.Newborn monkeys were separated from their mothers as part of an experiment investigating domoic acid, a neurotoxin produced by marine algae that accumulates in shellfish and can cause illness in humans. Researchers tested whether exposure to the toxin before birth damaged the infants’ brains. To do this, they dosed 32 pregnant macaques every day. After birth, 28 infants were taken from their mothers, bottle-fed, kept in incubators and later housed alone from the age of three weeks.In the heart-breaking video, the baby monkeys are seen sucking their fingers, screeching and jerking as scientists shave their heads and check their reflexes and memory.Dr Lisa Jones-Engel, Peta’s chief science adviser on primate issues, described the distressing conditions the infant monkeys endured during the experiments. “These monkeys are so young they still have the distinctive black fur of newborn macaques, yet instead of clinging to their mothers, they grasp blankets on metal tables,” the adviser told The Guardian. Jones-Engel spent 17 years as a primate scientist at the university before becoming one of its most outspoken critics. She has spent 35 years working as a primatologist.The project ran from 2014 to 2020 and received more than $4.2 million in funding from the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Some experiments lasted years. Peta says the monkeys were killed once the work ended. The research programme has operated at the university’s infant primate lab since 1971.Macaques are social animals that live in groups in the wild. Maternal care is essential for their social and behavioural development, Dr Malene Hansen, a long-tailed macaque expert, told the publication.Responding to concerns over the treatment of the infant monkeys, the Washington National Primate Research Center told The Guardian: “We recognise that research involving infant animals raises important questions about their wellbeing. Maternal relationships and early social development are important considerations in nonhuman primate welfare. Our experienced veterinary and animal care personnel have specialised expertise in primate care, including nursery rearing. ”The NIH said it places a high priority on laboratory animal welfare. “All animals used in NIH-supported research are protected by laws, regulations and policies designed to ensure the smallest possible number of animals are used and their welfare is prioritised.”The WaNPRC said it is not currently conducting studies involving infant monkeys, although approved protocols for such research remain active.Infant monkeys cannot thrive without their mothers, making separation itself unethical. “It is unethical to conduct research that separates infant macaques from their mothers. Period,” Hansen added.Jones-Engel makes a similar point about the reasoning behind the work. “There is no moral escape hatch. You can’t claim primates are used because they’re so like us, then take an infant away from its mother and experiment on it. You would never do that to a human primate. The cruelty also has biological consequences: maternal separation alters an infant’s physiology, immunity, behaviour and development, distorting its response to the very substance or disease being studied. ” Jones-Engel’s transition from animal researcher to campaigner is documented in the new film Sentient.Jarrod Bailey, a research scientist, argues that biological differences often mean monkey experiments fail to produce treatments for human diseases, including HIV/AIDS, Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. “We pay the price in failed treatments; monkeys pay with their lives. A shift away from monkey experiments would benefit all primates, including humans.”This footage offers a rare glimpse into experiments involving monkeys. Jones-Engel added: “For decades, the term ‘primate research’ has obscured the reality inside laboratories. These videos expose the suffering and raise a fundamental question: why are these facilities still operating at all?”The university says it is working to replace, reduce and refine animal experiments, although it maintains that “animal studies remain necessary for some complex scientific questions”. Peta is calling for the closure of all seven US National Primate Research Centers. “This is the same facility where Beth Buffalo deprives elderly monkeys of food and water to compel them to stare at a computer screen for up to nine hours in exchange for drops of juice, claiming this allows her to understand how the brain ages,” Peta said. The animal rights group has urged the public to share its video on social media and take action to help shut down the Washington National Primate Research Center.In the US, federal agencies are moving towards alternatives to reduce animal testing, including new approach methodologies such as organ-on-a-chip technology and computer modelling. Even so, more than 106,000 monkeys were held in US facilities in 2025, up 1.5 per cent from 2024. Between 2025 and 2026, more than 32,000 primates were imported from Asia and Africa for laboratory use, the publication said.
Article Summary: Newly released footage shows infant macaques subjected to neurological tests at the University of Washington’s National Primate Research Center. The video offers the first filmed look inside these experiments. It shows tiny monkeys shrieking in fear and gripping blankets, their only form of comfort. Researchers tested whether exposure to a neurotoxin in the womb damaged their developing brains.

Article Title: London's Natural History Museum won a landmark legal fight to reduce its annual rental value from £12.92 million to just £1; the decision could reshape how national museums are taxed
Article Text:
Natural History Museum on Cromwell Road, South Kensington, London. Image Credit: Wikipedia

The Natural History Museum won its landmark business rates challenge

Why was the museum considered unsuitable for commercial valuation

Importance of this ruling for other museums

How could the decision ease financial pressure on cultural institutions

London’s Natural History Museum has won a landmark legal challenge that reduced its rateable value for business rates from £12.92 million to just £1, marking a significant development for publicly funded cultural institutions across England. The Valuation Tribunal for England ruled that the museum should not be assessed as though it were a profitable commercial property, given its financial position and commitment to free public admission. The decision has since prompted a change in the government’s approach to valuing free-entry museums and galleries, potentially bringing substantial financial relief to institutions facing rising operating costs.The Natural History Museum’s successful appeal centred on how its property should be valued for business rates. According to the Museums Association, the museum was initially assigned a rateable value of £12.92 million in the 2017 Rating List. This was subsequently reduced to £4.16 million using a method based on the estimated cost of rebuilding the property. The museum challenged that assessment, arguing that a nominal valuation of £1 better reflected the economic realities of operating the institution.The Valuation Tribunal for England heard the case over two days in February 2026 and issued its decision in March. The ruling established that the museum’s rateable value should be reduced to £1, effective from 1 April 2017. The initial work on appealing the decision was subsequently abandoned, allowing the judgment to stand.As explained by law firm Mills & Reeve in its analysis of the ruling, the tribunal considered whether the museum could realistically be operated profitably by a hypothetical tenant. Its findings supported the museum’s argument that its specialist buildings, collections and public-service responsibilities made it fundamentally different from an ordinary commercial property.The decision was particularly significant because the museum became the first national museum in the UK to win such a business rates challenge.The tribunal’s decision rested on the distinction between a commercial property and an institution whose primary purpose is public service. The Natural History Museum preserves and displays collections, conducts scientific research and provides free access to visitors. Its operations are not designed to generate the profits expected from a conventional commercial enterprise.Mills & Reeve explained that the museum’s financial accounts demonstrated that it could not operate profitably, even with government grant funding. The tribunal also concluded that there was no realistic prospect of a commercially motivated organisation taking on the building under the same conditions.The valuation dispute involved the receipts and expenditure method, which examines an organisation’s income and operating costs to determine the rent a hypothetical tenant might reasonably pay. The tribunal accepted that this was the appropriate approach for the museum.However, the assessment could not rely on speculative income that the institution did not actually receive. The government funding provided to the museum was conditional on free public admission and could not simply be treated as rental income available to a hypothetical commercial tenant.The tribunal also declined to give decisive weight to hypothetical admission charges and other assumptions about how the museum might operate differently. Its actual financial performance provided a more reliable basis for determining the property’s value.The implications extend well beyond the Natural History Museum. According to the Museums Association, free-entry museums and galleries across England are expected to benefit from a change in the way their business rates valuations are calculated.Following the tribunal decision, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport confirmed that the Valuation Office would stop using the notional receipts approach when assessing free-entry museums where that method had previously been applied.Under the earlier approach, assessors could estimate hypothetical ticket revenue by considering visitor numbers and an assumed admission charge, even when the museum offered free entry. For institutions that depend heavily on public funding and have limited income from other sources, these calculations could produce valuations that did not reflect their actual financial circumstances.The October report explained that the government’s revised approach followed the tribunal’s rejection of notional receipts in the Natural History Museum case. HM Revenue and Customs confirmed that the change in rating case law would need to be reflected across the museums and art galleries sector where the approach had been used.Several museums had already established relevant legal precedents. These included Exeter’s Royal Albert Memorial Museum, Tyne and Wear Archives and Museums, now known as North East Museums, and York Museum and Gallery Trust. The Natural History Museum’s victory extended this line of decisions to a major national institution.The revised valuation approach could help museums redirect money previously allocated to business rates towards their core responsibilities. Maintaining historic buildings, caring for collections, conducting research and providing public access all require substantial resources.The Museums Association highlighted the potential for significant backdated savings for the Natural History Museum following the reduction in its valuation. The decision could also provide other museums and public bodies with grounds to review their own business rates liabilities.However, a reduction to £1 is not guaranteed for every institution. The Museums Association noted that HMRC expects some museums to retain higher valuations where their receipts and expenditure demonstrate a surplus.The Valuation Office will also consider reliable rental evidence where it is available, as this is regarded as a more accurate indicator of a property's rateable value.
Article Summary: The Valuation Tribunal for England heard the case over two days in February 2026 and issued its decision in March. The ruling established that the museum’s rateable value should be reduced to £1, effective from 1 April 2017. The initial work on appealing the decision was subsequently abandoned, allowing the judgment to stand. According to the Museums Association, free-entry museums and galleries across England are expected to benefit.

Article Title: Saudi Arabia offered Houthis $1 billion through Iran to stop attacks: Report
Article Text:
Saudi Arabia rejects ‘military blackmail’ as $1 billion Houthi deal is reported

Saudi Arabia has reportedly offered $1 billion to Yemen's Houthi group under an Iran-brokered arrangement aimed at securing a ceasefire and stopping attacks on the kingdom, Israeli media reported, citing diplomatic sources in the Gulf.According to the reports, Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman travelled to Tehran for talks on a possible ceasefire with the Houthis. The proposed arrangement reportedly involved transferring $1 billion to the group through Iran.One diplomatic source claimed that the Saudi minister had even brought the money to Tehran aboard the Hercules military transport aircraft he arrived in. However, a Saudi official did not confirm that any money had been transferred, the reports said.The talks reportedly brought together Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin and Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir , alongside Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Supreme National Security Council Secretary General Mohsen Rezaei and senior officials from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).According to the reports, Iran offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis amid escalating attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, which have caused economic damage to the kingdom.Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz have also disrupted oil exports from the Gulf, adding to regional instability.The Saudi foreign ministry addressed the visit in an official statement, saying, "The visit to Tehran by Prince Khalid bin Salman, the defence minister, and representatives of the member states of the Mecca Joint Defence Alliance comes as part of the 'Nato-style' alliance's ongoing efforts to de-escalate tensions between the parties to the current crisis, encourage dialogue and diplomatic solutions, and support the mediation efforts undertaken by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. "A Saudi official, speaking to Israeli media, did not confirm the reported financial transfer but said that part of the dispute with the Houthis centred on the implementation of understandings reached three years ago.Under those understandings, Saudi Arabia was to provide direct financial assistance to the Houthis as part of efforts to reach a settlement. The funding was intended, among other purposes, to pay public-sector salaries in areas under Houthi control and rebuild civilian infrastructure. In return, the group was expected to maintain the ceasefire and stop attacks on Saudi Arabia, the reports said.In recent months, the Houthis have sought to justify their "attacks" by alleging that Saudi Arabia reneged on the earlier understandings.However, the Saudi position reportedly remains that the kingdom will not agree to a new ceasefire under "military blackmail". Israeli media reported that Riyadh also opposed transferring funds to the Houthis before they returned territory seized from Yemen's internationally recognised government, which Saudi Arabia backs.The reported negotiations come amid wider regional tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel. Tehran has sought to strengthen its regional influence while promoting a security framework led by regional powers.According to Israeli media, the Tehran meeting also marked the first official meeting between representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Alliance and the Iranian leadership. The initiative reportedly took shape during the Pakistani army chief's visit to Tehran the previous week.The reports said Iran was seeking to position itself as a regional diplomatic mediator while opposing US or Israeli military intervention in the region.The reported $1 billion proposal, including the claim that the money was brought to Tehran aboard the Saudi minister's aircraft, has not been independently confirmed.
Article Summary: Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman travelled to Tehran for talks on a possible ceasefire with the Houthis. The proposed arrangement reportedly involved transferring $1 billion to the group through Iran. Saudi position reportedly remains that the kingdom will not agree to a new ceasefire under "military blackmail"

Article Title: Brazil court orders defeated Flávio Bolsonaro to surrender passports, bars him from leaving
Article Text:
Flávio Bolsonaro

Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro has been ordered to surrender his passports within 24 hours and barred from leaving the country. The order comes after his dramatic defeat to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff.Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes issued the confidential ruling, which also prohibits Bolsonaro from contacting lawyer Willer Tomaz, who is being investigated alongside the senator in a suspected money-laundering case, Brazil’s public news agency Agência Brasil reported.Bolsonaro confirmed the passport order in a video posted on social media on Monday, saying he had been served with the notice after visiting his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest in Brasília.“I was ordered right on the street to hand over my passports, and I'm also prohibited from leaving the country,” Bolsonaro said in a social media video.He added that the decision was based on remarks made by his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who reportedly told a podcast last Friday that Flávio should leave Brazil if he lost the election.“I never said that,” Flávio Bolsonaro said, denying that he intended to flee the country.The ruling cancels all his passports, including the diplomatic passport he holds as a senator. It also forms part of a Federal Police investigation into suspected money laundering and illegal foreign exchange transactions involving Tomaz, a lawyer linked to betting companies under scrutiny.Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court and Federal Police did not immediately respond to requests for comment, according to reports.The development comes amid political uncertainty following Lula’s victory in the runoff. The official tally released by the Superior Electoral Court showed Lula winning 51.79 per cent of valid votes, against 48.21 per cent for Bolsonaro.The senator initially challenged the result, calling for the election to be annulled over an extension of voting hours intended to address disruptions caused by public transport stoppages and heavy rain. The extension was ordered to help eligible voters reach polling stations.“It is impossible” to recognise the results, Bolsonaro said, alleging unequal treatment of voters. His legal team had indicated that it would challenge the outcome, although the legal basis for annulment remained unclear.On Monday night, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party acknowledged the result in a statement, saying: “We recognise the presidential result proclaimed by the electoral court, but believe that the questions raised need to be properly clarified through a balanced and democratic political debate.”The passport restrictions add to the legal challenges facing Bolsonaro, who is also under investigation in a separate case concerning money allegedly sought for a biopic about his father. His Senate term is due to end early next year, potentially removing the special jurisdiction associated with his office.
Article Summary: Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro has been ordered to surrender his passports. The order comes after his dramatic defeat to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The ruling cancels all his passports, including the diplomatic passport he holds as a senator.

Article Title: Five years after Rangers manager Walter Smith died, his widow Ethel chose the cancer unit that treated him to receive £50,000 from a charity, one of the biggest donations in the Scottish hospital's hi
Article Text:
Cancer unit that cared for Walter Smith

A charity established after a personal loss

Walter Smith's legacy beyond football

Five years after former Rangers and Scotland manager Walter Smith died following a battle with cancer, his widow Ethel has chosen to honour his memory by directing a £50,000 charitable donation to the hospital unit that cared for him. The gift, made through the Emmie Smillie Foundation, was presented to the cancer unit at Vale of Leven Hospital in Alexandria, Scotland, on October 26, 2026, the fifth anniversary of his death.According to STV News, Ethel nominated the unit in recognition of the treatment and support her husband received there. The donation is among the largest the hospital has received and will be used to improve facilities and make treatment more comfortable for patients. Hospital officials said the exact plans for spending the money were still being determined when the gift was announced.“When I was asked where I would like the money to go, I had no hesitation in nominating the unit here at the Vale,” Ethel said, explaining that the family wanted to acknowledge the care provided by the hospital. “Walter received treatment here, so it felt fitting as a thank you for the care we received from the unit and the hospital in general,” she added.The donation was formally presented to June Raines, the unit's charge nurse, and Gerry O'Hare, a former clinical nurse specialist who cared for Smith during his treatment. The contribution will support the unit's work serving patients from across the surrounding region.Vale of Leven Hospital is located in Alexandria, West Dunbartonshire, and provides cancer treatment and other services to patients in the west of Scotland. Its haematology-oncology unit offers day-care treatment, allowing many patients to receive care close to home without requiring an overnight hospital stay. According to Scottish News, the unit has 12 treatment chairs and a phlebotomy service. Its treatments and support include chemotherapy, blood transfusions and symptom management for people with cancer and blood disorders.For the Smith family, the hospital's importance went beyond its medical services. Ethel's decision to nominate the unit reflected the personal experience of receiving care during a difficult period. Gerry O'Hare, who now works part-time at the Beatson in Glasgow, said the donation would help support a service that had meant a great deal to Smith and his family.“Having worked at the Vale and knowing personally how much the unit meant to Walter and his family, it is wonderful to see such a significant donation coming back to support its patients,” O'Hare said, according to STV News. He added that the service was important to the local community and welcomed the foundation's contribution towards its continued work.June Raines also thanked the foundation, noting that the unit's ability to provide treatment locally helped patients avoid travelling farther for care. She said the funding would allow the hospital to enhance its facilities and improve the experience of people coming in for treatment.The donation was made through the Emmie Smillie Foundation, established by businessman Andy Smillie after his daughter died from cancer. The foundation raises money to support cancer services across Scotland through charitable contributions and fundraising activities.The latest gift is not the first time the organisation has supported Vale of Leven Hospital. STV News reported that the foundation had made a similar £50,000 donation to the hospital around four years earlier.The new contribution brings together two families' experiences of cancer and loss. The foundation was established in memory of Smillie's daughter, while Ethel's nomination reflects the care her husband received during his illness.The funding will be used to improve the hospital unit's facilities and patient experience, although the precise projects to be supported have not yet been announced. The hospital's leadership welcomed the donation, saying it would help staff continue providing compassionate care to patients and their families.Rebecca Reid, interim director for NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde's Clyde Sector, thanked the foundation and Ethel for selecting the hospital. She said the money would help the unit improve the experience of patients receiving treatment at Vale of Leven.Smith died aged 73 on October 26, 2021, following a battle with cancer. He remains one of the most respected figures in Scottish football, particularly for his achievements with Rangers, where he enjoyed two successful spells as manager. During his first spell at Ibrox, Smith won 13 major trophies in seven years before becoming Scotland manager in December 2004. He returned to Rangers in 2007 and added another eight trophies before retiring in 2011 after completing a domestic double.He also managed Everton and led Scotland's national team for three years. His achievements made him a defining figure in Rangers' modern history, while his influence extended to players and fellow managers who worked with him.The donation arrives as supporters and the club continue to remember Smith five years after his death. However, its significance lies not only in the football manager's legacy but also in the practical support it will provide to people receiving cancer treatment.By nominating the unit that cared for her husband, Ethel has ensured that the family's gratitude will translate into support for other patients facing similar challenges. The £50,000 contribution will help the hospital improve its facilities and treatment environment, allowing Smith's memory to be associated with care for the community as well as his achievements on the pitch.
Article Summary: Walter Smith died aged 73 on October 26, 2011, following a battle with cancer. His widow Ethel nominated Vale of Leven Hospital in Scotland to receive a £50,000 donation. The donation was made through the Emmie Smillie Foundation. The money will be used to improve facilities and make treatment more comfortable for patients.

Article Title: In 1985, Dionne Warwick, Elton John, Gladys Knight and Stevie Wonder recorded a charity hit; the song helped raise millions for AIDS research as the epidemic was unfolding
Article Text:
How four music legends came together

Why the song mattered during the AIDS epidemic

How much money did the charity hit raise?

The song's success continued at the Grammys

A musical legacy beyond the charts

In 1985, as the AIDS epidemic spread and fear and misinformation surrounded the disease, four of the biggest names in music came together to record a song that would become a landmark charity hit. Dionne Warwick, Elton John, Gladys Knight and Stevie Wonder joined forces on That's What Friends Are For, turning a song about friendship and support into a fundraising effort for AIDS research. Released under the name Dionne & Friends, the single became a major commercial success, eventually raising millions of dollars for the American Foundation for AIDS Research, known as amfAR. It also earned major Grammy recognition, giving the campaign a reach far beyond the recording studio.The song was written by Burt Bacharach and Carole Bayer Sager and had originally been recorded by Rod Stewart for the 1982 film Night Shift. When Warwick took up the song for the charity project, the idea developed into a collaboration featuring Elton John, Gladys Knight and Stevie Wonder.The performers brought together distinct musical styles, creating a recording whose message of loyalty and solidarity resonated with listeners.The project was supported by Bacharach, Bayer Sager and record executive Clive Davis, with proceeds directed towards AIDS research. The single was released in 1985, at a time when public understanding of HIV/AIDS remained limited and the need for research funding was urgent.In the early 1980s, AIDS had become a growing public-health crisis, but the disease was still widely misunderstood. The first recognised cases in the US were reported in 1981. Researchers were working to understand the virus, develop diagnostic tools and identify effective treatments, while people affected by the epidemic often faced discrimination and social isolation.A significant scientific milestone came in March 1985, when the US Food and Drug Administration approved the first commercial blood test to detect HIV. The test helped identify infections and made it possible to screen donated blood more effectively. However, effective long-term treatment remained unavailable, and the epidemic continued to claim lives.Against this backdrop, a charity recording featuring four internationally recognised performers helped bring AIDS research to a much wider audience. Its impact extended beyond its message: the commercial success of the single generated substantial funds for research and helped keep the cause in the public eye.The recording raised approximately $3.4 million for AIDS research, according to the Recording Academy's retrospective on Bacharach's career. Other accounts describe the total more generally as more than $3 million. The money supported amfAR, an organisation established in 1985 that became a prominent funder of AIDS research and an advocate for people affected by HIV/AIDS.The fundraising achievement was especially significant because the song reached audiences who might not otherwise have engaged directly with the issue. Its success demonstrated how the music industry could use a commercially popular release to generate money and attention for a public-health cause.That's What Friends Are For became a major hit in the US, reaching No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1986. It went on to win two awards at the 1987 Grammy Awards: Song of the Year, awarded to songwriters Bacharach and Bayer Sager, and Best Pop Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal, awarded to Warwick, John, Knight and Wonder.The awards cemented the recording's place in popular music history. But its legacy was not limited to chart positions or industry recognition. The song became closely associated with a moment when artists used their collective influence to support AIDS research at a time of immense uncertainty.The significance of That's What Friends Are For lies in the combination of its message, its star-studded collaboration and its fundraising impact. The recording did not solve the AIDS crisis or directly produce a medical breakthrough, but it helped finance research and raise awareness when both were urgently needed.Decades later, the song remains a prominent example of how popular music can support a charitable cause. Its message of friendship took on a broader meaning during the epidemic, offering a reminder of the importance of solidarity with people affected by a disease that was still poorly understood.
Article Summary: Dionne Warwick, Elton John, Gladys Knight and Stevie Wonder recorded That's What Friends Are For in 1985. The single became a major commercial success, eventually raising millions of dollars for the American Foundation for AIDS Research. It also earned major Grammy recognition, giving the campaign a reach far beyond the recording studio.

Article Title: The man behind ‘Over the Rainbow’ left a social justice legacy; his foundation now offers nonprofits grants of up to $5,000
Article Text:
Yip Harburg, PC: Wikipedia

Over the Rainbow lyricist Yip Harburg and his social justice legacy

Yip Harburg Foundation grants: eligibility and how to apply

Past grantees show the range of causes supported by Harburg’s legacy

More than 85 years after “Over the Rainbow” appeared in The Wizard of Oz, lyricist E.Y. “Yip” Harburg’s work continues to generate support for charitable causes. The Yip Harburg Foundation, established in 1981, uses royalties from his songs to fund nonprofit programmes pursuing economic and social justice. It offers grants ranging from $500 to $5,000 to eligible programmes operated by registered 501(c)(3) organisations with less than $10 million in assets. Its grants have supported work involving social and economic justice, immigration rights, climate change, criminal justice and underserved communities. Harburg wrote lyrics that addressed racism and social injustice, and he used humour to raise awareness of serious issues. The foundation’s grant programme gives a continuing charitable role to revenue from his songwriting, directing funds towards organisations working on social concerns.Harburg, who lived from 1896 to 1981, was described by the foundation as “Broadway’s social conscience”. Across a career spanning more than 50 years, he wrote lyrics for over 600 songs, including the songs in the 1939 film The Wizard of Oz. His best-known work, “Over the Rainbow”, won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.In 2001, Judy Garland’s performance of “Over the Rainbow” topped the Recording Industry Association of America’s “Songs of the Century” list. The project was created by the RIAA, the National Endowment for the Arts, Scholastic and AOL@School. According to CNN’s report on the list, hundreds of voters selected songs from a pool of 1,100 supplied by the RIAA and the National Endowment for the Arts, with space to write in additional choices.Harburg also wrote songs that addressed economic hardship and war. “Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?”, written with composer Jay Gorney in 1932, became closely associated with the Great Depression. The 1937 musical Hooray for What!, created with composer Harold Arlen, carried an anti-war message, while Bloomer Girl (1944), also written with Arlen, explored feminist and anti-racist themes. His political views affected his career. During the McCarthy era, Harburg was blacklisted from film, television and radio from the early 1950s for roughly a decade. He continued writing for Broadway. The foundation’s biography of Harburg describes his use of wit to “gild the philosophic pill”, using humour to convey ideas to audiences.The foundation awards grants of $500 to $5,000 to programmes operated by registered 501(c)(3) organisations with less than $10 million in assets. According to its official grant guidelines, an organisation may apply once per year, whether or not it received funding previously. Applications are reviewed quarterly, with meetings held in December, March, June and September. Applicants do not need to email to confirm receipt of an application. The foundation says it will notify applicants whether they have received funding and invites them to check back if they have not heard anything within 3 months of submitting their application.The foundation’s published grant statistics show about 30% for social and economic justice, 30% for immigration rights, and 40% for other areas, including climate change, criminal justice and underserved communities. Organisations considering an application can review the foundation’s mission and funding information to assess whether their work fits its stated priorities. The official grants page provides the application requirements and access to the online application form.The foundation’s published list of previous grantees includes organisations working in legal advocacy, environmental protection, medical debt relief, immigration and the arts. Recipients named on the site include the Coalition of Immokalee Workers, The Bail Project, the Midwest Innocence Project, Rainforest Action Network, the Outlaw Ocean Project and RIP Medical Debt. Arts organisations such as Black Ensemble Theatre and Theatre for the New City also appear on the list. These recipients work across different issues covered by the foundation’s grantmaking. The list includes organisations addressing criminal justice, environmental concerns, medical debt relief and artistic expression, among other causes.Established in 1981, the year Harburg died at the age of 84, the foundation is funded by royalties from his songs. The foundation’s website does not specify which songs generate the royalties. Its licensing page directs requests to the Yip Harburg Lyrics Foundation and the Songwriters Guild of America, separate organisations identified for licensing enquiries. The licensing information does not establish how royalties from individual songs flow to the grantmaking foundation. Harburg’s songwriting remains part of his legacy, alongside his work addressing social issues through lyrics and humour. Through its grants, the foundation continues to direct revenue from his songs towards nonprofit programmes working on economic and social justice.
Article Summary: The Yip Harburg Foundation uses royalties from his songs to fund programmes pursuing economic and social justice. It offers grants ranging from $500 to $5,000 to eligible programmes operated by registered 501(c)(3) organisations with less than $10 million in assets. Previous grantees include organisations working in legal advocacy, environmental protection, medical debt relief and immigration.

Article Title: An Indiana man threw rocks at his ex-wife's home and later set her fence on fire; despite guilty pleas, an October 23 appeals court overturned $15,017.50 in restitution orders because they were added
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Rocks thrown at ex-wife’s home followed by fence arson

Plea agreement left restitution open in only one case

Trial court ordered $15,017.50 in payments

Appeals court reverses restitution orders

A guilty plea does not give a court unlimited authority to change a sentence after it has been finalised. An Indiana man who admitted to damaging his ex-wife’s property has won an appeal against restitution orders totalling $15,017.50, after a court found that the trial judge lacked the authority to impose the payments months after sentencing.According to an October 23 memorandum decision by the Indiana Court of Appeals, available on Justia , the original sentencing orders did not require restitution or reserve the issue for later consideration. The appellate court reversed the orders and instructed the trial court to remove the unauthorised amounts from the relevant sentencing records, while leaving the man’s guilty pleas and convictions undisturbed.The case involved David McDonald, who faced criminal charges after two separate incidents involving his ex-wife’s property in 2025. In February that year, McDonald went to his ex-wife’s home and threw two rocks at the house. An active protective order prohibited him from contacting her. Following the incident, the State charged him with Class B misdemeanour criminal mischief.Later in 2025, McDonald returned to the property, poured gasoline on part of his ex-wife’s wooden fence and set it on fire. The incident led to a Level 6 felony arson charge, along with other charges.McDonald was also facing a separate Level 6 felony theft case involving his employer. He subsequently entered into a single plea agreement covering these and several other pending cases. Under the agreement, he pleaded guilty to criminal mischief and arson in the cases involving his ex-wife, as well as theft in the separate case involving his employer.The dispute centred on what the plea agreement allowed the trial court to decide after sentencing. According to the appellate decision, the agreement expressly left the amount of restitution in the theft case open for determination at a later hearing. It did not include a provision requiring McDonald to pay restitution to his ex-wife in the criminal mischief and arson cases.At the sentencing hearing, the State attempted to present evidence concerning restitution in the theft case. However, because McDonald’s former employer was not present, the trial court deferred the matter to a later hearing and proceeded to sentence him on the charges covered by the agreement. On February 4, 2026, the court entered sentencing orders in the criminal mischief and arson cases. Neither order mentioned restitution, and neither stated that the court was retaining authority to decide the issue later.The restitution question returned before the trial court on May 6, when a hearing was scheduled in the separate theft case. During the proceedings, the prosecution sought to address restitution for the damage to McDonald’s ex-wife’s property as well. McDonald’s defence objected, arguing that the hearing was scheduled only for the theft case and that the plea agreement did not leave restitution open in the other cases. The trial court nevertheless proceeded to consider the claims.Following the May hearing, the trial court ordered McDonald to pay his ex-wife $3,760 for the criminal mischief case and $11,257.50 for the arson case. Together, the two orders totalled $15,017.50. The trial court later amended the arson sentencing order following a June 3 hearing on McDonald’s motion to correct his credit time. However, the amended order also included the $3,760 restitution amount in its monetary obligations section.McDonald challenged the restitution orders before the Indiana Court of Appeals, arguing that the trial court had already entered final judgments in the criminal mischief and arson cases and therefore lacked the authority to add restitution afterwards. The State argued that the trial court had indicated during the earlier proceedings that restitution would be addressed later. The appellate court rejected that position, noting that the discussion at sentencing concerned restitution for McDonald’s employer in the theft case, not payments to his ex-wife.The Indiana Court of Appeals concluded that the trial court lacked the authority to impose restitution in the criminal mischief and arson cases after entering final sentencing orders. The judges explained that restitution forms part of a criminal sentence and that a trial court cannot ordinarily modify a sentence without continuing authority provided by the judgment, a statute or a rule. In McDonald’s case, the original sentencing orders did not reserve the restitution issue, and the plea agreement contemplated restitution only in the theft case.The appellate court also clarified that the agreement’s reference to an open plea did not give the trial court unrestricted discretion. The only unresolved matters were the amount of restitution in the theft case and where McDonald would serve 365 days of his sentence. The court therefore reversed the restitution orders and remanded the cases with instructions to vacate the $3,760 criminal mischief order and the $11,257.50 arson order. It also directed the trial court to amend the arson sentencing record to remove the $3,760 amount from the monetary obligations section.The decision did not overturn McDonald’s guilty pleas or convictions for criminal mischief and arson. It addressed the trial court’s authority to impose the additional payments after sentencing. The October 23 ruling was issued as a memorandum decision and, under Indiana Appellate Rule 65(D), is not binding precedent for any court. It may be cited for persuasive value or to establish res judicata, collateral estoppel or law of the case.
Article Summary: David McDonald admitted to damaging his ex-wife's property in 2025. He pleaded guilty to criminal mischief and arson in two separate cases. He was ordered to pay $15,017.50 in restitution in both cases. But the Indiana Court of Appeals overturned the orders. It found the trial judge lacked the authority to impose the payments.

Article Title: 3-year-old Florida boy escorted from soccer match after parents claim he was dropped for outplaying 5-year-olds and being 'too good'; police called to the scene
Article Text:
How a 3-year-old's soccer skills sparked controversy

What the league official told police

Why police were called to the field

i9 Sports launches a review

Nevada's mother says the incident upset her son

Viral incident sparks debate over children's sport

A three-year-old boy named Nevada Pierre has gone viral after a dispute at a youth soccer game in Winter Park, Florida, led a league official to call the police. Videos shared by his family show the toddler dribbling past older opponents and scoring goals, prompting his parents to allege that he was being excluded because he was too good at the game. The league official, however, told officers that Nevada had allegedly pushed other players and that his parents had argued with him over playing-time decisions. Police responded to Martin Luther King Jr. Park on October 24, 2026, and spoke to both sides. The incident attracted widespread attention after body-camera footage and videos of the match circulated online.Nevada was playing in a youth soccer programme run by i9 Sports, competing against children around five years old. Videos posted by his family show him controlling the ball, dribbling past opponents and scoring goals.His mother, Martasia Griffin, claimed that other parents were unhappy with his performance because their children struggled to take the ball away from him. In a social media post, she alleged that the league had removed her son because he was outperforming the older players.The videos quickly gained traction online, with viewers questioning why a recreational sports programme would exclude a young child over his playing ability.However, the disagreement also involved allegations about physical play and the parents' interactions with league officials.In police body-camera footage, league official Thomas Hayes acknowledged that Nevada was exceptionally skilled for his age but alleged that the boy pushed other players while scoring goals.Hayes told officers that he had tried to discourage pushing and had rotated children during games to give everyone an opportunity to play. He also claimed that Nevada's parents had previously objected when their son was taken out of a game and that a disagreement developed after he asked referees to address the alleged pushing.Hayes told officers that the parents had argued with him and other parents. He requested that the family leave and said he was willing to refund their registration fee.Nevada's parents disputed his account. His mother told officers that she believed the league was excluding her son because he was good at soccer. The footage of the match shared by the family does not show the alleged pushing.The Winter Park Police Department said officers responded after a soccer league official reported a disturbance involving league staff and a player's parents. The official asked officers to speak with the family because he did not want the disagreement to escalate further.Police heard both sides of the dispute. The incident report recorded the official's concerns about the parents' behaviour and the family's belief that their child was being criticised for playing too well.Officers classified the incident as a civil matter rather than a criminal one. According to the department, the family said the game was over and that they were leaving. They cooperated with officers, and no arrests were made.Police also clarified that nobody was formally trespassed or forced to leave the park. Although the league had requested that the family leave and offered a refund, officers did not forcibly remove them from the premises.The local i9 Sports programme acknowledged the controversy after videos of the incident spread online. The organisation said it had contacted the family and begun reviewing the circumstances, including speaking with those involved.In its statement, i9 Sports emphasised that the respectful treatment and well-being of children and their families were important to the organisation. It also said it would not speculate or share unverified information while the review was under way.The organisation's statement did not confirm that Nevada had been excluded because of his playing ability or establish whether the allegations about pushing were substantiated.The dispute has raised questions about how youth sports leagues should manage differences in ability, playing time and sportsmanship, particularly when very young children compete against older participants.Griffin said the experience had been distressing for Nevada and that she was concerned he might believe he had done something wrong. She maintained that the family had enrolled him to play soccer and that his ability should not have become a reason to exclude him.The family shared additional footage of the match on social media, challenging the allegation that Nevada had pushed other players. The posts attracted widespread support and prompted discussions about the responsibilities of adults running recreational sports programmes.The controversy also caught the attention of former NFL quarterback Robert Griffin III, who criticised the situation publicly. Children's entertainer Rachel Griffin-Accurso, widely known as Ms. Rachel, also expressed support for Nevada and invited him to appear on her show.The family has received considerable online backing, while the league's review remains central to determining how the dispute developed and what led to the decision to end Nevada's participation.The incident has prompted a broader discussion about balancing competition, fair playing time and sportsmanship in youth sports. Some social media users questioned why police were called to a disagreement involving a three-year-old, while others highlighted the need for organisers to address concerns about physical play and the conduct of adults at children's matches.Recreational leagues often have to accommodate children with different levels of experience and ability. Organisers must also ensure that young participants have opportunities to play, learn the rules and develop their skills in a safe environment.In Nevada's case, the family maintains that his talent led to his exclusion, while the league official cited alleged pushing and conflict with the parents. Police treated the matter as a civil dispute, and i9 Sports said it was reviewing the incident.
Article Summary: Nevada Pierre was playing in a youth soccer programme run by i9 Sports. Videos posted by his family show him controlling the ball, dribbling past opponents and scoring goals. His mother, Martasia Griffin, claimed that other parents were unhappy with his performance because their children struggled to take the ball away from him. The league official, however, told officers that Nevada had allegedly pushed other players and that his parents had argued with him over playing-time decisions.

Article Title: Jon Bon Jovi's Toms River restaurant welcomes diners who cannot afford a meal; in the first half of 2026, more than 80% of the meals it served went to guests experiencing food insecurity
Article Text:
How the pay-it-forward model works

Food assistance alongside other community services

Toms River's temporary pop-up served more than 15,870 meals

More than 80% of the meals served at Jon Bon Jovi 's JBJ Soul Kitchen restaurant in Toms River, New Jersey, went to guests experiencing food insecurity during the first half of 2026, according to the Jon Bon Jovi Soul Foundation. The foundation's announcement, published on its official website as part of a sponsorship appeal for the restaurant's annual Chilli Cook-Off, highlights the role of its community restaurant in providing nutritious meals to people who cannot afford them.Unlike conventional restaurants, JBJ Soul Kitchen does not list fixed prices on its menu. Instead, diners who can afford their meals are encouraged to make a suggested donation and contribute towards the cost of feeding someone else. Guests unable to pay are welcomed to enjoy a meal and learn about volunteering opportunities, according to the restaurant's official website. The approach is designed to address hunger while allowing people to dine in a setting that promotes dignity and community rather than treating food assistance as a separate service.JBJ Soul Kitchen is a nonprofit community restaurant established by the Jon Bon Jovi Soul Foundation, which was founded in 2006 to help break the cycle of hunger, poverty and homelessness.The restaurant's model brings together paying customers, volunteers and people experiencing financial hardship around a shared dining experience.Guests who can afford to pay are encouraged to make a suggested donation and cover the cost of another person's meal. Those unable to contribute financially can volunteer their time, with restaurant staff helping them explore opportunities to participate in the community. The arrangement is not a conventional pay-what-you-want system, according to the organisation, but a structured effort to connect meals with volunteering and community support.The restaurant serves a chef-prepared three-course meal, typically including soup or salad, a choice of entree and dessert or fruit. Menus change every two weeks, and ingredients are sourced locally where possible. The restaurant says it aims to ensure that nutritious food is accessible without making the ability to pay a condition for being welcomed at the table.The restaurant's work extends beyond providing meals. It collaborates with local organisations to connect guests with resources related to housing, mental health, substance-use support, employment and other essential needs.In a May 22, 2026, feature, the James Beard Foundation described how the restaurant uses food as an entry point for building relationships with people facing difficulties that may not be immediately visible. Founder and programme director Dorothea Bongiovi explained that creating a safe and welcoming environment can help guests feel comfortable discussing their circumstances and seeking assistance.The foundation's feature reported that 78% of diners across the restaurant's operations identified as being in need. It also described how community coordinators work with partner organisations in Monmouth and Ocean counties to connect guests with relevant services. These can include housing assistance, job training, addiction treatment, mental health support and help accessing public benefits.The 78% figure refers to diners identifying as being in need across the restaurant's operations, while the foundation's separate first-half-of-2026 statement specifically reports that more than 80% of meals at the Toms River location went to guests experiencing food insecurity.The restaurant's impact in Ocean County was also evident at a temporary JBJ Soul Kitchen pop-up inside the Ocean County Library in downtown Toms River. Launched in February 2025 at the library's invitation, the initiative aimed to respond to the growing needs of people experiencing homelessness and expand access to meals and community support during the winter Code Blue season.The pop-up closed on April 30, 2026. Before closing, it had served more than 15,870 meals over the previous year, with 79% going to guests in need, according to JBJ Soul Kitchen. More than 1,000 volunteers contributed nearly 4,000 hours of service during the initiative.The programme also connected guests with support beyond food. According to the organisation, it distributed more than 1,350 hygiene kits and made 276 referrals to service providers. These efforts resulted in 13 successful housing placements and nine people securing employment. The figures were also reported by News 12 New Jersey in April 2026.Although the library pop-up has closed, the organisation confirmed that its permanent Toms River restaurant on Hooper Avenue would continue operating. The temporary site's results demonstrate how the same pay-it-forward approach can be extended to meet needs in a specific community, particularly when food insecurity overlaps with homelessness and limited access to essential services.JBJ Soul Kitchen's approach aims to make food assistance part of an ordinary restaurant experience. Rather than separating people who need help from those who can pay, the model encourages them to share the same space and meal.The Jon Bon Jovi Soul Foundation received the 2026 James Beard Foundation Impact Award, recognising its work addressing hunger, poverty and homelessness. The award brought wider attention to the organisation's community-based approach and the role its restaurants play in connecting people with both meals and support services.
Article Summary: More than 80% of meals served at JBJ Soul Kitchen in Toms River, New Jersey, went to guests experiencing food insecurity during the first half of 2026. The Jon Bon Jovi Soul Foundation's community restaurant does not list fixed prices on its menu. Instead, diners who can afford their meals are encouraged to make a suggested donation and contribute towards the cost of feeding someone else. Guests unable to pay are welcomed to enjoy a meal and learn about volunteering opportunities.

Article Title: In 2017, South Carolina sent a 168-foot bridge that carried traffic since 1939, 50 miles offshore; the reef drew grouper and billfish to a once-sandy seafloor
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing a retired steel highway bridge resting on a barge structure on the Atlantic seabed, where fish gather around the artificial reef. Credits - Gemini

From highway to seabed

Grouper and billfish

AI-generated representative image showing a retired steel highway bridge secured to a marine barge for transport to an offshore artificial reef site. Credits - Gemini

Why states sink old structures

Bridges do not last forever, and many are eventually sent for scrap. South Carolina chose a different fate for an old Highway 41 bridge in 2017. After carrying traffic over the Wando River near Charleston since 1939, the steel span was repurposed as part of an offshore artificial reef, where it provides habitat for marine life. The steel swing bridge once connected Mount Pleasant with the area near the Francis Marion National Forest across the Wando River. It measured 168 feet (about 51 metres) in length. After the replacement bridge opened, the old span was cleaned and attached to a retired barge. The combined structure was taken about 50 miles (80 kilometres) off Charleston and deployed in more than 300 feet (91 metres) of water as part of the South Carolina Memorial Reef. It was placed on the seabed rather than buried beneath sediment, adding hard structure and habitat to a previously sandy stretch of ocean floor.In August 2017, the old bridge was removed as vehicles began using the replacement span nearby. Crews lowered the old structure by crane onto a barge and cleaned it to remove materials that could harm the marine environment. The bridge was then secured to a retired barge measuring 130 feet long.The combined structure was deployed at the Charleston Deep Reef in October 2017, providing 44 feet of vertical relief above the seabed.The project required substantial funding as well as engineering work. The South Carolina Department of Natural Resources estimated the cost of purchasing, cleaning and transporting the structure at $180,000, with contributions expected from conservation groups and private donors. The Memorial Reef fund was established by independent anglers seeking to honour family members and friends through artificial reef projects. The South Carolina Governor’s Cup Advisory Board worked with the department to support the initiative.
