Article Title: Were they beheaded? Did they get lawyers? Bangladesh seeks answers from Saudi Arabia over execution of 'couple'
Article Text:
Bangladesh seeks answers from Saudi Arabia over execution of two citizens

Dhaka seeks details of charges, trials and executions

Discrepancy over charges and sentences

Bangladesh has sought detailed information from Saudi Arabia about the execution of two of its citizens in the Makkah region, including the charges against them, court verdicts, method of execution and whether they had legal representation during their trials, according to a media report.The Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah sent a diplomatic letter to the Saudi ministry of foreign affairs' branch in Makkah on October 19, seeking answers to six questions, Bangladeshi newspaper Prothom Alo reported on Sunday.Bangladesh's consul general in Jeddah also raised the matter with a senior Saudi foreign ministry official during a meeting on the same day, the report said.The two Bangladeshi nationals, a man and a woman, were executed on October 14 after being convicted of committing an “indecent act” inside a mosque in Makkah.In its diplomatic communication, Bangladesh sought details of the offences for which the two citizens were convicted, including when and where the alleged acts took place. It also requested their arrest dates and certified copies of the court verdicts, Prothom Alo reported.Dhaka has asked Saudi authorities whether the death sentences were carried out by beheading or another method. It has also sought information about the whereabouts of the bodies and whether they would be repatriated to Bangladesh or had already been buried in Saudi Arabia.The letter further asks whether lawyers represented the two citizens during the investigation and trial, and whether they had sought legal assistance.Bangladeshi officials said the country's diplomatic missions did not have detailed information about the legal proceedings leading to the executions, including whether the two individuals had been represented by lawyers.Saudi authorities had not responded to the consulate's latest diplomatic communication, the newspaper reported, citing Bangladeshi officials.Dhaka is also seeking clarification over information contained in a list of Bangladeshi prisoners shared by Saudi authorities in September.The list reportedly included allegations of adultery and an information technology-related offence involving the two citizens. However, it did not specify their sentences.Bangladesh is seeking an explanation for the discrepancy between those entries and the Saudi interior ministry's public explanation of the executions.The Bangladeshi government had also raised the matter with the Saudi ambassador in Dhaka, according to the Dhaka Tribune.Bangladeshi officials said the government had not received detailed official information from Saudi authorities before learning that the executions had taken place, the newspaper reported last week.Dhaka has also sought details about 20 other Bangladeshi citizens whose names appeared on the Saudi prisoner list as convicted, but whose sentences were not specified.The latest diplomatic communication comes as Bangladesh seeks further information about the circumstances surrounding the October 14 executions and the legal proceedings against the two citizens.
Article Summary: Bangladesh seeks details of charges, trials and executions. Consulate General in Jeddah sent a diplomatic letter to the Saudi ministry of foreign affairs' branch in Makkah on October 19. The two Bangladeshi nationals, a man and a woman, were executed on October 14 after being convicted of committing an “indecent act” inside a mosque in MakKah. Bangladesh has asked Saudi authorities whether the death sentences were carried out by beheading.

Article Title: In first-ever climate crisis amends, Nepal to get $21.6 million
Article Text:
A drone view shows houses covered in mud after the flash floods and mudslide in Nepal.

NEW DELHI: Marking its first response to a climate change-induced loss and damage event, a UN body has decided to provide $21.6 million to Nepal that faced catastrophic flash floods in Aug, triggered by a massive rock-ice avalanche and a partial glacier collapse.The decision taken this week by the UN body, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), in its emergency meeting assumes significance as it is not only a kind of admission that climate change causes such extreme events, but also an endorsement of the principle that historical polluters (developed nations) must contribute to the fund to assist vulnerable developing countries.The purpose of this fund, created under the UN climate change framework, is to assist developing countries that are particularly vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change. The fund was established at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, in 2022 and operationalised at COP28 in Dubai, UAE, in 2023.“This is a historic first step, but it cannot be a one-off. No country should have to endure a catastrophe and wait seven weeks just to unlock the Fund’s first-ever emergency meeting. We must set up a permanent rapid-response system that moves support in days, not months,” said Harjeet Singh, a climate change expert and the global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign.
